https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/17/amer.text: Menü Kereső Négy napig áram, légkondi és működő WC nélkül vesztegelt a tengeren egy amerikai hadihajó Külföld Csurgó Dénes Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Valószínűleg kevesen cserélnének helyet a USS Benfold romboló hadihajó 281 fős legénységével, akik négy napig áram, légkondicionálás és WC nélkül maradtak a hajójukon a Dél-kínai-tengeren. Az eset még július végén történt, amikor a hajón rutinfeladatok közben meghibásodott a hajó generátora, így a 150 méter hosszú hadihajó teljesen áram nélkül maradt. Az áramkimaradás azt jelentette, hogy nem működött sem a konyha, sem a légkondicionáló rendszer, ahogy a mosdók sem, sőt, az ivóvízellátással is problémák adódtak. Az amerikai haditengerészet közleménye szerint a matrózok kitartóan és profin kezelték a helyzetet, de hogy mit kezdtek például a négy nap alatt felgyülemlett dolgokkal, arról nem osztottak meg részleteket. A USS Benfold legénysége nem maradt azért étlen-szomjan, a vele egy kötelékben hajózó Robert Smalls cirkálóról ugyanis adtak enni és inni a matrózoknak. Négy nappal a meghibásodás után aztán egy felbérelt vontatóhajó elérte a megrekedt rombolót, és azt a Fülöp-szigeteken található Subic-öbölbe vontatta, ahol a megfáradt legénység végre elhagyhatta a hajót és vehetett egy hosszú fürdőt. Két nappal később sikerült megjavítani a generátort, ezután a hajó Japán felé vette az irányt. Hogy milyen pokoli megpróbáltatásoknak van kitéve a legénység az amerikai haditengerészet hajóin , arról itt írtunk részletesebben. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ‘It’s very special to have something from here,’ said Savannah, left. ‘Everyone seems very excited,’ said Maria, right. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian Barbican Monstera magic: Barbican hands out cuttings as ‘green lung of the city’ closes Five hundred people turn up to adopt plants from conservatory that will reopen in 2030 after renovation project Helena Horton Thu 20 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A bove the waxy monstera leaves and bright pink hibiscus flowers in the Barbican conservatory hangs a giant net to catch the panes of glass that are at risk of falling from the ceiling on the unwitting plant lovers below. This precarious situation has caused the estate to shutter its greenhouse on the third and fourth floors for three years so a full refurbishment can take place. But the hiatus has a silver lining for many of those who visited on Wednesday to give the plants from the conservatory a new home. View image in fullscreen The conservatory refurbishment is part of the wider Barbican renewal programme, a £231 million renovation of the site. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian Five hundred people turned up to pick up a cutting from the Barbican’s plant collection and were asked to fill out an “adoption form” as if they were taking home a pet. Lydia Goldberg, 56, a tech worker, was one of the first through the door and selected a pretty, silvery-green Swedish ivy plant. “I am a houseplant lover,” she said. “I live in the Barbican and my bedroom overlooks the conservatory. I am sad to see it close but it’s great that it’s being restored. Having a piece of the conservatory in my flat will be incredible and this is a real community event. I can see quite a few of my neighbours here!” View image in fullscreen 'This is a real community event,’ said Lydia Goldberg, who lives on the Barbican estate. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian The Swedish ivy is among the plants being sorted by the head gardener, Marta Lowcewicz. She was fizzing with excitement as queues of people began to file in. “There has been a social media storm,” she said. “It is amazing how much interest there has been!” There are going to be three adoption events, each giving away 500 cuttings from species in the conservatory. The first, held this week, ran out of free online tickets almost immediately. View image in fullscreen Five hundred people turned up to choose a plant cutting at the first event. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian Part of Lowcewicz’s job is to figure out which plants will remain indoors and which will go outside. The climate has changed considerably since the Barbican was built in the 1960s and many indoor plants are now outdoor plants. “Some of the plants are a bit rough around the edges after the weather we have had,” she said. London has sizzled in five heatwaves and the climate control in the conservatory has not caught up. “When we have new climate control and irrigation systems, the plants will be healthier.” Lowcewicz will be choosing new plants for the collection, but says “we are looking to retain as many of our plants as possible”. She will select plants that have “big, bold leaves”. “The architecture of the Barbican is striking and bold so we are trying to make sure the collection fits well with the concrete. We want them to soften it,” she said. View image in fullscreen Tickets for the first ‘adoption’ event sold out online almost immediately. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian There are plants from all over the world in the conservatory and Geoffrey, a 36-year-old spatial designer, selected one that reminded him of Mexico, where he used to live. “I chose a white velvet plant, I love it. I am a great fan of the building and it is great to take a piece of it home with me.” Savannah, 33, and Maria, 30, were grinning with delight and holding their cuttings. “I chose the peperomia,” said Savannah, who works with elderly people. “I love the texture of it, it’s very soft. I have a ton of plants, but I love the Barbican so it’s very special to have something from here.” Maria, an architectural designer, chose the trailing purple heart plant. “I have lots of houseplants but this is my first non-green plant!” she said. “I am having a great time. Everyone here seems very excited, everyone loves plants. I will keep my new plant on my bookshelf.” View image in fullscreen Prospective plant-parents were asked to fill out an ‘adoption form’, much as if they were taking home a pet. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian Visitors milled around the brutalist space as they waited to pick up their cuttings. Stella, 88, lives in the Barbican and chose a Benghal dayflower. “I like it because it has a little secret blue flower,” she said. “I have houseplants everywhere and am meant to be cutting back but, really, how can you resist this?” Stella has given some of her houseplants that grew too big for her flat to the conservatory, including a giant monstera. “It’s huge, I hope they don’t give it back to me!” View image in fullscreen ‘How can you resist this?’ said Stella, who lives in the Barbican and took home a Benghal dayflower – but did not want her giant monstera back. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian The event was bittersweet, as most people were rueful that the space will be shut for such a long stretch. Dr Philippa Simpson, the chief operating officer of the Barbican, feels keenly the responsibility of faithfully restoring the conservatory, which means a lot to lovers of brutalist architecture and plants alike. “It’s a green lung of the city,” she said. “We are undertaking a massive restoration of it because it was in urgent need of rescue. We have nets up to deal with falling glazing, massive waterproofing issues. It is leaking into all of our significant spaces.” When the conservatory reopens in 2030, it will be fully accessible – as it is not currently, for those with limited mobility – and will be open seven days a week rather than during limited hours. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Railway workers respond to a call to repair overhead lines after they were destroyed by a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv region. Photograph: Jelle Krings View image in fullscreen Railway workers respond to a call to repair overhead lines after they were destroyed by a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv region. Photograph: Jelle Krings Ukraine Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital Luke Harding and Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.23 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died , with a dozen wounded, including three children. “An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky . View image in fullscreen Boryspil, in the Kyiv region. Trains were evacuated and travellers stranded during Russia’s days-long air assault on Kyiv Photograph: Jelle Krings The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days , beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families. Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland. View image in fullscreen Railway workers repairing overhead lines after a Russian strike. Photograph: Jelle Krings Serhih Leshchenko , a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company. For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences. Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged. Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook , the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead. View image in fullscreen A destroyed railway bridge in the Lyman district in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk oblast. Photograph: Jelle Krings “It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted. She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.” Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers. Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “ The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Refugees arriving in Lviv on evacuation trains from Kharkiv and Kryvy Rih make their way through the train station. Photograph: Jelle Krings Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said. Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said. Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi. View image in fullscreen A wounded Ukrainian soldier is evacuated on a train. Photograph: Jelle Krings On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train. ‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villages Read more In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop. Pertsovsky , Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote. https://rollcall.com/2026/10/13/bipartis.text: Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, attend a Senate Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee hearing on June 2. They are among six Republican senators who signed a letter opposing the Russian diesel purchases deal. ( Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call ) By John M. Donnelly Posted October 13, 2026 at 4:51pm, Updated at 7:32pm A dozen senators from both parties bluntly told President Donald Trump in a letter Tuesday to reverse a deal he announced last week to allow U.S. purchases of Russian diesel fuel. The proposed waiver of U.S. energy sanctions on Russia would permit the purchase of several hundred thousand tons of the fuel from that country, beginning “immediately,” the president said in an Oct. 9 social media post stating his aim is to ease high energy prices for Americans. Since then, congressional critics of the deal from both parties have sounded off against it, never more resoundingly than in Tuesday’s letter from six Republicans and six Democrats, including some of the chamber’s most powerful members. “This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded,” the senators wrote. The letter’s signatories included high-ranking Republicans such as Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who chairs the Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, chairman of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. Also signing were Democratic ranking members Sens. Jack Reed of Rhode Island from Armed Services, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire from Foreign Relations and Chris Coons of Delaware from the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. Other Defense appropriators who signed were Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill. Also signing were GOP Sens. John Cornyn of Texas, who serves on the Foreign Relations and Intelligence panels; Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma; plus Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, a member of the Armed Services Committee; and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. Russia sanctions The waiver for Russian diesel provides Vladimir Putin, that country’s president, with finances for his “war machine,” the senators wrote, which “enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians.” The action stands to damage U.S. security interests “and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war.” Another Republican Defense appropriator, Sen. Jerry Moran of Kansas, criticized the president’s action in a post on X on Monday, saying: “We should be tightening sanctions further, not undercutting them by allowing the import of Russian diesel and risking erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries.” To critics, Trump’s decision to allow U.S. purchases of Russian diesel runs counter to a measure he signed into law just under a month ago that would impose new sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, in addition to those already on the books. Additionally, critics contend that the 2022 law titled the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act prohibits the administration from importing Russian oil unless the president certifies that Russia has withdrawn from Ukraine, poses no threat to NATO and recognizes Ukraine’s sovereign right to exist. Top energy experts have noted in recent days that U.S. imports of Russian diesel would have little impact on the overall supply of the fuel in the United States — but could deliver billions of dollars to the Russian government. Question of legality The new Senate letter came two days after seven senators, including some of the same ones who signed Tuesday’s missive, issued a statement that effectively called Trump’s move illegal. “Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” the senators wrote. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies.” That statement was penned by Republican Sens. Collins, Murkowski, Tillis and John Curtis of Utah, a member of the Foreign Relations Committee; plus Democratic Sens. Shaheen, Blumenthal and Ron Wyden of Oregon, a member of the Intelligence Committee. The seven senators said the decision “runs directly counter to that law,” and they said the administration has also “failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.” House GOP misgivings In the House, meanwhile, GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, who is in a tough reelection race in a district Trump lost in 2024, vowed in an X post on Oct. 10 to file bipartisan legislation soon “to block any and all purchases of Russian oil.” He said he would force the measure to the House floor via a discharge petition and predicted “it will pass overwhelmingly.” Even as Fitzpatrick clashes with the administration on its Ukraine policies, The New York Times reported Tuesday that two top GOP super PACs have shifted campaign funds from three faltering Republican candidates to other races, including Fitzpatrick’s contest. The outcome of his race could affect GOP hopes of holding the House majority. Another maverick House Republican, Don Bacon of Nebraska, who is retiring after this session, has repeatedly criticized Trump’s Russian diesel waiver. “Buying Russian diesel violates U.S. law,” he said in a post on X that linked to the seven senators’ statement. Most Americans, Bacon said in another post , “reject buying fuel from Russia that funds the bombing of cities.” Despite the pushback from Republican hawks, other senior Republicans declined to criticize the president’s move. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” that Trump is “balancing his effort to stop and end … Putin’s war in Ukraine and lowering prices for American families.” Likewise, House Majority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said on ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday that Trump’s decision on Russian diesel is “another example of our president thinking out of the box. You know, he’s listening to the American people.” View from Europe In Ukraine, meanwhile, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in an unusually barbed comment about a U.S. policy, called Trump’s action on Russian fuel a “weak decision by strong partners” and a “gift” to Putin, telling ABC News’ “This Week” on Sunday: “It gives Putin money and he spends money only on this war.” Trump’s approval of U.S. purchases of Russian diesel comes as European officials have said the Kremlin is behind a rash of sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and online disinformation across the continent. In a sign of the growing tensions, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s top commander and head of U.S. European Command, said in a speech to the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday that the alliance is prepared to rebuff any Russian invasion. Trump administration officials have reportedly pushed Ukraine to halt their increasingly successful strikes on energy infrastructure inside Russia. Trump has suggested that these strikes are driving up world energy prices, which have risen largely as a result of the war in the Persian Gulf. This report was corrected to accurately characterize statements by Sen. John Barrasso and Rep. Tom Emmer.
